title: South Sudan: what we built before running a single session
excerpt: Announcing an expansion is easy. This is the unglamorous part — registration, employment law, safeguarding routes, cash handling and security — because that is what decides whether a program survives its second term.
body:
JdiobeSTEM Foundation is extending its school programs into South Sudan. Announcing an expansion is easy. This article is about the unglamorous part — registration, employment law, safeguarding routes, cash handling and security — because that is the part that decides whether a program survives its second term.

## Why South Sudan

We already work in Uganda and the United States. School partnerships run in Uganda, and now in South Sudan.

The case is not complicated. There are secondary students in South Sudan who can reason carefully and who have never had anyone show them what an engineer actually does. The constraint is not talent. It is that almost every input a science program normally assumes — a working laboratory, a reliable supplier, a road that is passable in the rains, a phone signal — cannot be assumed.

So we designed for its absence rather than complaining about it. Our programs already run without mains electricity and without an internet connection. That was a choice made for rural Uganda, and it is what makes South Sudan possible at all.

## What is actually in place

**Registration.** JdiobeSTEM Foundation is a registered 501(c)(3) nonprofit organization in the United States, registered to operate in South Sudan with the Relief and Rehabilitation Commission (RRC). Keeping that registration, and any State or County agreement required where we work, current is a named duty of one person, not a shared aspiration.

**Employment law.** Staff in South Sudan are employed under the Labour Act, 2017 (Act No. 64 of 2017). We wrote a country-specific contract rather than translating the Ugandan one, because the two statutes differ on notice, leave and overtime. Our template carries a standing rule: it may only improve on the Labour Act, never reduce it. Where the Act gives a better term than the contract, the Act wins.

**Governance.** The constitution, the conflict-of-interest register, the meeting and resolution templates and the safeguarding undertaking were all drafted before the first school visit, not after the first problem.

## The 80% rule is the point, not an obstacle

The NGO Act 2016 requires that a minimum of 80% of an NGO’s employees, at all levels, are South Sudanese citizens, and that the ratio is reported.

We are not going to pretend that is a compliance burden we are gracefully absorbing. An organization that needs a legal instrument to make it hire nationals has already lost the argument. A South Sudanese teacher knows which roads flood, which head teacher answers a phone, and what a family will and will not say in front of a stranger. We could not buy that knowledge if we tried.

The rule is reported on at every level, including management. We treat the ratio as a measure of whether the country program is genuinely local, not as a threshold to clear.

## One person accountable

South Sudan is run by a Country Coordinator who reports to the Executive Director. The role holds the school relationships, delivers or supervises the programs, and accounts for the money.

It is worth being explicit about what that person may *not* do, because the limits are the safeguard:

- They do not sign a partnership agreement or a lease. The Executive Director signs.
- They do not commit the organization to costs above a written limit.
- They do not travel, or send anyone else to travel, against the security advice. No session is worth it, and no report is late enough to change that. The decision to stop is recorded either way.
- **They do not make a facilitation payment of any kind.** If somebody asks for one, they refuse it, record it, and tell the Executive Director the same day.
- They do not hold parent or guardian consent. The school holds it.
- They do not approve their own expenses.

That last set is short and blunt on purpose. Every line of it exists because organizations working in hard places have broken it.

## Money, in a currency that moves

The country program runs on a float in South Sudanese pounds. Every transaction is recorded, every receipt kept, and the exchange rate used on the day is recorded with the transaction — not reconstructed later from a monthly average. Accounts reconcile monthly with the Finance and Administration Officer in Uganda.

Materials are sourced locally where possible. Where they must come from outside, long lead times are planned for, and the Coordinator is expected to say *in advance* when something will not arrive in time rather than explain afterwards why a session did not run.

## Safeguarding, and an honest gap

Our standard is the same in every country: an adult from the school is present at every session, no JdiobeSTEM person is ever alone with a learner, and any child protection concern is reported within 24 hours. The school holds guardian consent — we do not collect it.

Two country-specific pieces are being finalized before delivery begins: the external reporting route for a concern raised in South Sudan, and the local security advice source used for go/no-go decisions. In Uganda the reporting route runs to the Police Child and Family Protection Unit, the district probation and social welfare officer and the national child helpline. South Sudan needs its own named equivalents, and a policy that names no one is not a policy.

There is also a gap we would rather state than paper over. As at July 2026 South Sudan has no comprehensive data protection law and no designated authority. We therefore apply the Ugandan standard there voluntarily. Children’s data does not become less sensitive because a statute has not caught up.

## What changes in the programs, and what does not

The four programs are the same: Research, Science Fair, Scholarships and Mentorship. The delivery model is the same — everything runs through the school, which provides a room, a timetabled slot, lockable storage, an adult at every session and a named focal point teacher. We pay no money to schools and we do not build parallel institutions.

What changes is the recording. Location is captured as State and County rather than district. Where it is relevant we record whether a learner is from a refugee or a host community, which matters more in South Sudan and in Uganda’s refugee-hosting districts than anywhere else we work. Registers, session records and attendance summaries use the identical forms to Uganda, so the figures combine into one set of national and cross-country totals rather than two incompatible spreadsheets.

Materials adapt to what is locally available. The method does not.

## What we are not claiming

We have not yet run a term of programming in South Sudan. We are not going to describe intent as achievement.

What we will report, when there is something to report, is the same measure we hold ourselves to in Uganda: how many students submitted a project proposal, how many were funded, and how many finished and filed a final report with receipts attached. Not attendance at a launch.

## Get in touch

Schools in South Sudan interested in a partnership, and organizations already working in education there, should write to [info@jdiobestem.org](mailto:info@jdiobestem.org) or call +1 405-437-4755.

Schools apply on one form. We visit before anything is signed.

title: What a wing teaches: JdiobeSTEM at the third Laudato Si' Green Festival
excerpt: We brought model aircraft, rockets and vehicles to Wanyange, put them on a table, and let students take them apart. This is what happened, and what we learned from it.
image_alt: Model aircraft and a rocket model laid out on the JdiobeSTEM exhibition table at the Green Festival
caption: The JdiobeSTEM table at the third Laudato Si' Green Festival, Holy Cross Lake View Senior Secondary School, Wanyange

gallery.alt: Visitors and students gathered around the rocket and aircraft models on the exhibition table
gallery.caption: Students and visitors around the rocket models

gallery.alt: A student-built model of a solar-powered irrigation system, with seedlings in wooden planting boxes
gallery.caption: One of the youth-led eco-innovation exhibits shown alongside ours

gallery.alt: Students holding a certificate of appreciation in front of a Holy Cross Lake View and Laudato Youth Initiative backdrop
gallery.caption: Certificate of appreciation, Holy Cross Lake View Senior Secondary School

body:
On Friday 11 July 2026, JdiobeSTEM Foundation exhibited at the third Laudato Si’ Green Festival at Holy Cross Lake View Senior Secondary School in Wanyange, Jinja. We brought model aircraft, rockets and vehicles, put them on a table, and let students take them apart. This is what happened, and what we learned from it.

## The festival, and our part in it

The third Laudato Si’ Green Festival ran over two days, 10 and 11 July 2026, organized by the Laudato Si’ Club of Holy Cross Lake View Senior Secondary School under the Laudato Youth Initiative. Its theme was *Environmental Conservation for Peace and Sustainable Development*.

JdiobeSTEM was there for one of those days. The first day, 10 July, was given to a community clean-up across Wanyange and Bugembe; we were not part of it. We came on 11 July, the main day, to run the STEM practical exhibition alongside the youth-led eco-innovation exhibitions and research showcases.

That distinction matters to us. We are one partner among several in an event we did not organize, and the credit for the festival belongs to the club that built it and to the Laudato Youth Initiative that carries it.

## A table, and what was on it

The exhibition was led by Dr. Muwanika Jdiobe, our Executive Director. He is an aerospace engineer in research and development at The Boeing Company and a STEM educator at Oklahoma State University, and he holds a PhD in aerospace engineering; his doctoral research was on unmanned aerial vehicles using ducted counter-rotating propellers — work aimed at making drones quieter and more efficient.

He also grew up in Jinja. The exhibition took place a short drive from where he went to school.

On the table were model aircraft, rocket models and model vehicles. Nothing was behind glass and nothing was demonstrated from a distance. Students picked the models up, turned them over, and asked why a wing is shaped the way it is. Several arrived with their questions already written down.

Nothing on the table required mains electricity or an internet connection. That was a deliberate choice, and it is the whole argument of a practical exhibition: the equipment is not the point. The reasoning is available to anyone willing to measure something, write the number down, and try again.

## The question the teachers asked

Students asked about lift, drag and noise. Teachers asked a harder question, and asked it more than once: *how does a school with no laboratory teach any of this?*

We came to Wanyange to answer exactly that. A school does not need a laboratory to teach a student to state a question precisely, predict what will happen, measure it twice, and write down both numbers even when they disagree. That is the discipline our Research program is built on, and it survives a power cut.

## The rest of the day

The second day opened with a Green Walk through Wanyange and closed with the Care for Creation Mass, celebrated by Fr. Peter Caxton Mayanja, C.S.C., Provincial of the Congregation of Holy Cross in East Africa. The one-million-tree planting drive was extended with Catholic parishes in Busoga.

Between the walk and the Mass sat the part of the programme that is hardest to photograph: the sustainability dialogues, which ran three strands at once — science, community, and mental health. That pairing is unusual and, we think, correct. A young person who is frightened about the future does not need another lecture on carbon.

Hon. Justine Kasule Lumumba, Uganda’s Minister of Information and Communications Technology, spoke about putting artificial intelligence to work in environmental stewardship. Fr. Mayanja returned to storytelling, arguing that ecological awareness travels through stories people recognize rather than through figures they have no way of checking.

Sarah Kirikumwino, President of the Laudato Si’ Clubs, put the point of the whole day more plainly than anyone:

> “We plant trees whose shade we will never sit beneath. We tend the soil that others will harvest.”
>
> — Sarah Kirikumwino, President of the Laudato Si’ Clubs

The Laudato Youth Initiative also launched the Bishop Charles Martin Wamika Moral Formation and Good Use of Technology Legacy Program, on youth moral development and the responsible use of the internet and new technology. Those two things belong together. Every student who asked us about drones also asked, in one form or another, what stops somebody using one badly.

## What we took away

The useful thing we noticed was not a number. It was that students who came to our table *after* sitting in a dialogue asked sharper questions. Somebody who has just heard about wetland encroachment asks a different question about drainage from somebody who has not.

That is the argument for holding a science exhibition inside a festival about creation, rather than on its own. Science answers “how”. The festival was asking “why”, and “for whom”. Students who have both in their heads at once ask better questions than students who have only one.

We are following up with the students who asked about the Science Fair and Research programs.

## Who made it happen

Organized by the Laudato Si’ Club of Holy Cross Lake View Senior Secondary School under the Laudato Youth Initiative, based at the John Paul II Justice and Peace Centre, Kampala. Fr. Prosper Atukwatse, C.S.C. hosted at the school.

Partners on the ground: Bethany Lands Institute, Foresters HSE Consults, Avail Fruits of Faith Farm, the Congregation of Holy Cross East Africa Province, and JdiobeSTEM Foundation. Vatican News carried the festival in English and Kiswahili.

For context, the festival has grown: the first, in 2023, drew more than 1,000 young people; the second, in 2025, drew more than 1,700 in person and more than 4,000 online.

## Working with us

Schools apply for a partnership on one form, and we visit before anything is signed. There are no fees, and no money passes to the school. Students apply to the Science Fair themselves, online, with a real budget and prices from real shops.

Write to [info@jdiobestem.org](mailto:info@jdiobestem.org) or call +1 405-437-4755. More on the Laudato Youth Initiative at [laudato-youthinitiative.org](https://laudato-youthinitiative.org/).

title: New scholarship support for Mbabazi Liz Lourine at Holy Cross Lake View SSS
excerpt: For Liz Lourine, this new support means more than financial help; it opens a path to confidence, opportunity, and growth in science-led learning through the Dr. Ron and Cara Beer STEM Scholarship.
image_alt: Mbabazi Liz Lourine during a scholarship-related school activity
caption: Mbabazi Liz Lourine, scholarship recipient at Holy Cross Lake View SSS
body:
The Jdiobe STEM Foundation is pleased to share a new scholarship support story for Mbabazi Liz Lourine, a student at Holy Cross Lake View SSS in Jinja. She has been awarded a scholarship through JdiobeSTEM Foundation under the Dr. Ron and Cara Beer STEM Scholarship, supporting her studies in BAF - Biology, Agriculture, Food and Nutrition / SubICT, a course that strengthens practical knowledge and future opportunities in science and applied learning.

This new support reflects our continued commitment to helping young people access quality education, build confidence, and grow their potential through STEM-related learning and academic encouragement. It is a reminder that practical support, when paired with opportunity, can transform a student’s future.

title: Jdiobe STEM Foundation awards travel scholarship to future aeronautical engineer
excerpt: At a time when travel costs can stand between talent and opportunity, our foundation stepped in to help a promising student begin a life-changing academic journey.
caption: Moses Nambiro, recipient of the Jdiobe STEM Foundation travel scholarship
body:
The Jdiobe STEM Foundation is proud to announce the award of a $1,000 travel scholarship to Moses Nambiro, a student from Uganda who has been admitted and awarded a scholarship to pursue a Bachelor of Science in Aeronautical Engineering. This support helps remove a major obstacle that often stands between gifted students and world-class education.

While Nambiro successfully secured admission and academic funding, additional financial support was required to cover travel expenses. Through this scholarship, the Jdiobe STEM Foundation is supporting his airfare from Uganda to Alegría, enabling him to begin his academic journey with greater confidence and less financial strain.

This award reflects the Foundation’s mission to remove barriers and expand access to STEM education for talented individuals globally. By addressing critical gaps such as travel costs, the Foundation ensures that opportunity is not limited by circumstance and that young people can pursue ambitious futures in science and engineering.

> “We believe that talent is universal, but opportunity is not. Supporting students like Nambiro is central to our mission of empowering the next generation of engineers and innovators.”
>
> — Dr. Muwanika Jdiobe

The Jdiobe STEM Foundation congratulates Moses Nambiro on this achievement and looks forward to his future contributions to the field of aeronautical engineering.
